newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RTZ-CRA seen exiting low-yield coal assets.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RTZ-CRA seen exiting low-yield coal assets.

text.p: A poor coal price settlement by Australian producers with Japan for 1997/98 is helping fuel market belief the RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd group may sell its Hunter Valley coal operations in New South Wales (NSW).
CRA's official position, through spokesman Ian Head, was that the talk was "fanciful speculation".
But well-placed Australian coal industry sources and stockbrokers' analysts told Reuters on Wednesday that a sellout was a definite possibility.

An exit by RTZ-CRA from Hunter Valley coal would primarily involve sale of the group's 71 percent stake in the A$700 million Coal and Allied Industries Ltd (CAIL), Australia's leading semi-soft coking coal producer.
A source close to CAIL said that, while talk of an RTZ-CRA sellout was speculation, lack of productivity and of returns on the group's coal investments were "pretty unsatisfactory".
This had been heightened by poor results achieved by Australia in its negotiating round with Japan for prices in the 1997/98 Japanese fiscal year (JFY), which begins on April 1.
The average price of hard coking coal to be sold to the Japanese steel mills in 1997/98 was effectively unchanged, Queensland miner QCT Resources Ltd said in December.

Leading coking coal producer, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, also announced in mid-December it had negotiated modest price increases at the premium end of the hard coking coal market while prices for lower quality coals had decreased.
"It's disappointing, given the fundamentals seemed to be favouring the suppliers," a coal industry executive said.
Settlements reflected a desire by major producers, headed by BHP, to maintain tonnages and were flowing through to semi-soft coking coal producers, headed by Coal and Allied, he said.
Semi-soft prices were emerging from Tokyo negotiations at rollover prices to A$2.00 a tonne less than last year, he said.
Steaming coal prices are still under negotiation with Japan with final prices heading toward a fall of A$2.00 to A$5.00 a tonne on 1996, another coal industry source said.
"Some new projects impacted on it (settlements) (and producers were) protecting their patch," he said.
Soft coking coal from BHP's new Mount Owen project in the Hunter Valley was sold at a substantial discount to the market, he said.
BHP announced in mid-December that it would sell 11 million tonnes of coking coal to the Japanese steel mills for JFY 1997, equally split between hard coking and weak coking coal.

"The reality is that because of the exchange rate and the lack of profitability in the operations and lack of productivity improvements, the returns to shareholders are pretty unsatisfactory," a source said of CRA's coal operations.

CAIL is presently looking at ways in which it can bring its own Hunter Valley mines and CRA's adjacent wholly-owned Novacoal together to produce synergy and rationalisation, Ian McPhee, CAIL's executive general manager marketing, told Reuters.

A study now beginning was expected to be completed in several months, he said. Total output of the two operations would be about 14 million tonnes a year, with CAIL contributing about 11 million tonnes.
CRA has also had its Kembla Coal and Coke assets in NSW on the market for some time.
Ube Industries LTD, Nissho-Iwai Corp and Joban Kosan Co Ltd together hold 20.7 percent of CAIL while the remaining shares are publicly held.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-12 9373-1800
